🥔 Notable quotable ... President Trump told reporters in the Oval Office that U.S. strikes on Iran are now "intermittent": "A lot of people don't call it a war. I call it a military conflict because it's small potatoes for us — it's not a big thing. We did Venezuela, and we did this." Watch the video.
 
 
1 big thing: The all-about-me campaign
 

Photo illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios. Photo: Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images
 

President Trump is hitting the campaign trail and doing the last thing many Republicans want: making the 59 days to the Nov. 3 midterms a referendum on him, Axios' Marc Caputo reports.

  • Why it matters: Most Republicans are too scared to bluntly tell Trump how unpopular he is. Timidity aside, Republicans need Trump's low-propensity voters to turn out. So they're going along with a Trump-focused strategy that many believe could cost them credibility — along with seats in the House and Senate.

"We have no choice. We're stuck on the boat with him whether we like it or not," said a top Republican campaign official who's in contact with Trump's political operation.

  • "Now, a rising tide raises all boats," the official added. "But the only ones who sound sure about the tide rising is the White House."

🐘 Coming attractions: At Trump's urging, the GOP on Wednesday and Thursday will host an unprecedented midterm convention in Dallas, headlined by the president.

  • Trump plans to appear both nights, with Vice President JD Vance as keynote on Wednesday and Trump on Thursday.

📱 Trump is also the star of his political operation's first two TV ads:

  • The first 30-second ad, "Toughest Guy," is all about you-know-who.
  • The second, "Tax Cut Prices," features Trump and would be more conventional for a campaign in which he's on the ballot.

📺 Inside the room: Trump essentially demanded the ads focus on him because midterms are referendums on a president anyway, and he wanted to tout his accomplishments, The Atlantic first reported (gift link).

  • "I'm not on the ballot, but I'm on the ballot," Trump told one confidant who relayed the conversation to Axios.
  • A Trump adviser told Axios: "Our job is to turn Trump voters into midterm voters."

🔎 The intrigue: The ads, however, are a de facto compromise between Trump and his political staff.

  • "This is for the audience of one," Trump's confidant said, referring to the president. "If the boss wants it, he gets it."
  • One Trump adviser said to expect more conventional ads: "We will be stripping the bark off of Democrats and supporting our candidates. ... It's not all Trump-focused ads."

🔎 Between the lines: Trump's message in his tax cut ads is good, Republican strategists say, but their research increasingly shows voters blame him for the war in Iran that's raising gas prices.

  • "Diesel's at an all-time high. Gas is about $4 a gallon. We can't message that away," said another Republican who runs campaigns for a few federal candidates.

🔮 What's next: At a Rose Garden dinner Wednesday with dozens of House Republicans, Trump promised to campaign across the country in 35 races "to see if we can get everyone elected."

  • If Trump wants to campaign for a candidate, it's going to be hard for them to say no, said one of the consultants involved in talks with MAGA Inc., the super PAC that backs Trump.
  • "Say no to Trump, and he could punish you," the consultant said. "Say yes to him, and his presence might not help. This is the world we're in."

2. 🐘 GOP confidence crash
 
Data: University of Michigan Surveys of Consumers. Chart: Mike Zapler/Axios

Another in a long list of ominous indicators for President Trump heading into the final two months before Election Day:

  • Republicans' confidence in the economy has plummeted over the last six months at a pace unseen since COVID — reminiscent of the declines during the global financial crisis nearly two decades ago, Axios' Mike Zapler reports.

🧮 By the numbers: Republicans still have a much more positive outlook on the economy than Democrats. But since February, Republican consumer sentiment has plunged 15.1 index points, from 97.1 to 82, according to the latest University of Michigan Surveys of Consumers data. Democratic sentiment has fallen just 1.6 index points, from 41.8 to 40.2.

  • The 82 reading is lower than at any point during either of Trump's presidencies, with one exception: December 2020, after he'd lost reelection but before he left office.

3. 🪖 Pentagon's major leak hunt
 
Photo: J. David Ake/Getty Images

Federal investigators "have taken the extraordinary step of subjecting roughly 50 members of the U.S. military's Joint Staff to polygraph tests over leaks to journalists, including about how the Iran war has created a shortage of crucial munitions," the N.Y. Times' Jonathan Swan, Adam Entous, Maggie Haberman and Eric Schmitt report.

  • The polygraphs were conducted in August, after news reports detailed diminished stocks of crucial munitions, including long-range missiles and Patriot interceptors, The Times said.

Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell told the paper that the department "does not comment on internal personnel or investigative matters but takes all leaks of classified national security information extremely seriously and investigates accordingly."

  • "Securing classified information is critical to ensuring the security of the United States and of our troops deployed around the world," he said.

4. 🏟️ College football frenzy
 
Data: NCAA, D1.ticker. Chart: Jim Sergent/Axios

College football's top tier — the NCAA Division I Football Bowl Subdivision — is on track to set an attendance record of 39 million this season, Axios' Jim Sergent writes.

  • Stunning stat: Attendance at 28 stadiums averaged at least 100% of their listed capacities last year, according to D1.ticker. Michigan led the nation, averaging 110,842 fans per home game, or 103% of the capacity of The Big House.
 
 
5. ⚡ OpenAI plans more disclosure on rogue agents
 
OpenAI image via X

OpenAI announced on X overnight that it plans to expand disclosures about incidents by rogue agents, following yesterday's Reuters report about a previously undisclosed breakout this spring.

  • "Historically, we have treated misalignment largely as a research question, which gets communicated in research publications such as system cards. This year, we've started to see misalignment cause new types of real-world impact," OpenAI said.
  • "We're working on a framework and will share it in upcoming weeks, and in parallel we're working with dozens of government regulatory agencies worldwide on these issues."

💡 Context: The AI agent breakout in Germany was detailed in a report shared ​exclusively with Reuters' Deepa Seetharaman and Raphael Satter by a group of researchers who uncovered the activity in late August while scouring ​the internet for signs of unauthorized AI-agent behavior.

  • The swarm of OpenAI agents hijacked a website and transformed it into a bulletin board for other AI agents.
  • The researchers found more than 15,000 edits by AI agents on a German-language wiki site, DseWiki, that's geared toward programmers and accepts communal edits à la Wikipedia.

6. 🍽️ Your local gem
 
The Astor, a 2,000-square-foot restaurant coming to Lower Manhattan, opens Sept. 15. Rendering: The Astor

"The most anticipated openings in the U.S. this fall are taverns, bistros, pizzerias and intimate neighborhood spots serving the kind of food diners already know they like," Bloomberg's Kat Odell writes.

  • Why it matters: Every restaurant wants to be your new neighborhood spot.

🥩 Case in point: New York City heavyweight chef Andrew Carmellini is opening The Astor at Lower Manhattan's Public Theater this month.

  • The Astor will serve American classics like deviled eggs and pigs-in-a-blanket. The average check is expected to be $75 a person. At the 2023 opening of another restaurant by the same chef, Café Carmellini, a single dish could cost that much.

Other big-time restaurateurs are also in on the trend:

  • Three-Michelin-starred Eleven Madison Park's Daniel Humm is opening Humm, a casual West Village spot, in October.
  • Michael Rafidi, chef of D.C.'s Michelin-starred Albi, is opening Bizzeria in Georgetown in November to serve up sourdough pies and mezze. "I like the idea of giving more accessibility to the community," Rafidi told Bloomberg.

7. 🏈 Stat du jour: Betting season
 

Illustration: Brendan Lynch/Axios
 

Americans are expected to bet $29.5 billion this NFL season through U.S. sportsbooks, according to the American Gaming Association. That's virtually unchanged from last year's $29.4 billion.

  • The intrigue: That number doesn't include the billions flowing through prediction markets like Kalshi, which are soaring in popularity. Sports wagers account for 80+% of bets placed on Kalshi, NPR notes.
 
 
8. ☕ 1 fun thing: Coffee competition
 

Illustration: Maura Losch/Axios
 

The long-reigning pumpkin spice latte has new rivals, Axios' Carly Mallenbaum writes.

  • Caramel, apple and cinnamon are the three most-ordered fall flavors on DoorDash, ahead of pumpkin, per data shared with Axios.
  • Searches for "caramel apple iced coffee" are at an all-time high, according to Google Trends.

Case in point: McDonald's dropped its longtime PSL and instead rolled out caramel apple pie coffee drinks this season, saying: "Step aside pumpkin spice, there's a new flavor in town!"
